title: 6 Questions Teachers Should Ask Before Implementing AI
author: Peter Greene
source: curmudgucation on Substack (originally at Forbes.com), December 10, 2025
summary: Greene opens with the political and financial weather driving AI into classrooms: a $50 million federal AI-literacy grant program, a White House task force, and a partnership between the AFT and AI vendors under the banner of a National Academy for AI Instruction. The framing is that teachers are being told, in effect, that refusal to adopt means being left behind, and the piece offers a set of questions a teacher should answer before taking the leap. Note for the archive: the email newsletter contains the first two questions in full and cuts off at "Read the full post here," with the remaining four questions behind the URL. The argument the two full questions make is substantive enough to stand on its own. Question one is the content-and-pedagogy audit. Greene uses Carl Hendrick's test-drive of ChatGPT for Teachers to show concretely what an AI lesson planner does and does not do. It does not survey the research on how best to teach a given topic, evaluate pedagogical approaches, and build a lesson on expert judgment. What it does, in the case Hendrick observed, is design lessons around learning styles, a debunked idea, and order the planning backwards: asking what activities might work before asking what students should learn. Greene's move is to refuse the magic framing. AI does some things well, but it is neither a content expert nor a pedagogy expert. Question two is the district-commitment audit. Veteran teachers already know the ed-tech cycle: low-cost entry, paid fee after year one or two, district exit, and a cohort of teachers who sat through the PD and built the program into their classroom now left to absorb the churn. Greene argues the AI wave looks particularly likely to run this cycle hard, because the industry is spending amounts of money it must at some point recoup. The implication for a teacher is to ask, before integrating an AI tool into assessment or lesson design, what happens to that integration when the fee arrives and the district decides to move on.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: The push is on for teachers to incorporate AI products in the classroom. The federal Department of Education has created a $50 million grant program to promote “AI literacy.” Melania Trump has launched a task force to push AI into classrooms.

The number of tools available to teachers is exploding, and teachers are regularly told that if they don’t join the revolution, they and their students will be left behind. But before a teacher implements AI tools in her classroom, here are some questions that she should consider.

If you use a chatbot to draw up lesson plans, here’s what it definitely does not do: it does not study the topic you want to teach, search through various pedagogical approaches being used, evaluate the most solid information, assess how best to conduct that instruction, and compose a lesson plan based on an expert’s grasp of the content and how to teach it.

Carl Hendrick… took ChatGPT for Teachers for a test drive and found that the program designs lessons around the idea of learning styles, a once-popular idea that students have modes (auditory, visual, kinesthetic, etc.) by which the best learn. It’s an educational myth that has been thoroughly debunked.

ChatGPT for Teachers also appears to do some lesson planning backwards, asking first “what activities can we best use with this content” instead of first asking what we want the students to learn and then what activities would best achieve that goal for that content.
There are some things that AI does well, but the program is not magic, and it is neither a content nor pedagogy expert.

Veteran teachers are familiar with an oft-repeated ed tech problem. The program is initially offered to the district at low or no cost, but a year or two later, the company will start to charge a real fee. Then the school district announces that they will drop the program. Teachers, who have sat through professional development and done the work of incorporating the program in their classroom, grit their teeth and brace themselves for the next big thing.

This cycle seems particularly likely with the AI industry, which is spending astonishing amounts of money that it must, at some point, make back.” Archived from curmudgucation on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
